stimulus.title: Social Science: When Should School Start?
stimulus.text:
Ask a teenager to fall asleep at nine o'clock at night and you are likely to be disappointed, not because of stubbornness, but because of biology. During adolescence, the body's internal clock shifts later. The hormone that helps signal that it is time to sleep begins to be released later in the evening than it was in childhood, so many teenagers simply do not feel tired until eleven o'clock or after.

At the same time, teenagers still need a great deal of sleep; most experts recommend somewhere between eight and ten hours a night. A student who cannot fall asleep before eleven and must wake at six to catch an early bus is, night after night, falling short. Sleeping late on weekends can make up some of the difference, but it also pushes the internal clock even later, making Monday morning harder still. Over a school year, the shortfall adds up.

The consequences are not trivial. Sleep-deprived students have more trouble paying attention, remembering what they learned, and controlling their moods. They are more likely to doze off in class and, for those old enough to drive, more likely to be involved in car accidents. Grades, too, can suffer when students arrive at their first class too tired to think clearly. Some research has linked chronic sleep loss in adolescence to higher rates of depression.

For these reasons, several major medical organizations have recommended that middle and high schools begin classes no earlier than 8:30 in the morning. Districts that have made the change have generally reported that students sleep longer on school nights, and some have reported better attendance and fewer students falling asleep in class. The change does not ask teenagers to become different people. It simply asks schools to fit the day to the students they actually have.

Adults sometimes respond that teenagers would sleep more if they put away their phones. Screens do make the problem worse, and good habits matter. But no amount of discipline will move a teenager's internal clock back to where it was at age ten.
stimulus.text_b:
I have read the research on adolescent sleep, and I do not dispute it. When our district's school board asked me to study whether we should move the high school's start time later, I expected the hardest part would be persuading skeptics of the science. Instead, the science turned out to be the easy part. The hard part was the buses.

Like many districts, ours uses the same fleet of buses and the same drivers for several routes each morning. The high school route runs first, then the middle school, then the elementary schools. Pushing the high school later would mean either hiring more drivers, who are already difficult to find, or pushing the younger children's start times earlier, which would put eight-year-olds at bus stops in the dark. Our transportation office estimated that even the cheapest workable plan would require several new routes. Neither option is free, and neither is simple.

Then there are the afternoons. A later start means a later dismissal. Our athletic teams already travel to games at schools with earlier schedules, and students would miss more class time to get there. Students with after-school jobs, many of whom help support their families, told us that a later dismissal could cost them hours of work. Parents who rely on older siblings to watch younger ones after school raised similar concerns.

I do not offer these complications as reasons to do nothing. Several neighboring districts have made the change, and their experiences suggest that many of the problems can be solved with time and money. Some found ways to arrange their routes more efficiently; others raised taxes to pay for additional drivers. My point is that a start time is not a single decision. It is connected to transportation budgets, labor markets, sports schedules, and family routines, and a change that looks obvious on paper can shift costs onto the people least able to absorb them.

Our board is still deciding. Whatever it chooses, I hope it chooses with all of those people in view.

When our district's school board asked me to study whether we should move the high school's start time later, I expected the hardest part would be persuading skeptics of the science. Instead, the science turned out to be the easy part. The hard part was the buses.

Like many districts, ours uses the same fleet of buses and the same drivers for several routes each morning. The high school route runs first, then the middle school, then the elementary schools. Pushing the high school later would mean either hiring more drivers, who are already difficult to find, or pushing the younger children's start times earlier, which would put eight-year-olds at bus stops in the dark. Our transportation office estimated that even the cheapest workable plan would require several new routes. Neither option is free, and neither is simple.

Then there are the afternoons. A later start means a later dismissal. Our athletic teams already travel to games at schools with earlier schedules, and students would miss more class time to get there. Students with after-school jobs, many of whom help support their families, told us that a later dismissal could cost them hours of work. Parents who rely on older siblings to watch younger ones after school raised similar concerns.

I do not offer these complications as reasons to do nothing. Several neighboring districts have made the change, and their experiences suggest that many of the problems can be solved with time and money. Some found ways to arrange their routes more efficiently; others raised taxes to pay for additional drivers. My point is that a start time is not a single decision. It is connected to transportation budgets, labor markets, sports schedules, and family routines, and a change that looks obvious on paper can shift costs onto the people least able to absorb them.

Our board is still deciding. Whatever it chooses, I hope it chooses with all of those people in view.

stimulus.title: Social Science: When Should School Start?
stimulus.text:
Ask a teenager to fall asleep at nine o'clock at night and you are likely to be disappointed, not because of stubbornness, but because of biology. During adolescence, the body's internal clock shifts later. The hormone that helps signal that it is time to sleep begins to be released later in the evening than it was in childhood, so many teenagers simply do not feel tired until eleven o'clock or after.

At the same time, teenagers still need a great deal of sleep; most experts recommend somewhere between eight and ten hours a night. A student who cannot fall asleep before eleven and must wake at six to catch an early bus is, night after night, falling short. Sleeping late on weekends can make up some of the difference, but it also pushes the internal clock even later, making Monday morning harder still. Over a school year, the shortfall adds up.

The consequences are not trivial. Sleep-deprived students have more trouble paying attention, remembering what they learned, and controlling their moods. They are more likely to doze off in class and, for those old enough to drive, more likely to be involved in car accidents. Grades, too, can suffer when students arrive at their first class too tired to think clearly. Some research has linked chronic sleep loss in adolescence to higher rates of depression.

For these reasons, several major medical organizations have recommended that middle and high schools begin classes no earlier than 8:30 in the morning. Districts that have made the change have generally reported that students sleep longer on school nights, and some have reported better attendance and fewer students falling asleep in class. The change does not ask teenagers to become different people. It simply asks schools to fit the day to the students they actually have.

Adults sometimes respond that teenagers would sleep more if they put away their phones. Screens do make the problem worse, and good habits matter. But no amount of discipline will move a teenager's internal clock back to where it was at age ten.
